The rules

The law

After the vote

What has to happen once a council's results are declared, how long it has, what can happen when no party has a majority, and what happens if a council misses its deadlines.

The timeline

  1. ResultsThe council is declared elected

    The IEC declares the result for each council. The 14-day deadlines below run from that declaration, so most new councils must meet and elect their leaders by late November.

    Structures Act ss 29(2), 45, 55
  2. Within 14 daysThe first meeting is called

    The municipal manager must call the new council's first meeting within 14 days after it has been declared elected. If there is no municipal manager, the provincial MEC for local government designates someone to do it.

    Structures Act s 29(2)
  3. First sittingA speaker is elected

    At its first sitting, the council must elect a speaker from among its councillors. The municipal manager presides over that election. The speaker then presides over the rest.

    Structures Act s 36
  4. Within 14 daysA mayor is elected

    A council with an executive mayor must elect one at a meeting held within 14 days of the council's election. A council with an executive committee must elect the committee's members within the same period, and then elects the mayor from that committee.

    Structures Act ss 45, 48, 55
  5. OptionalA whip

    The council may also elect a whip at its first sitting. The speaker presides over that vote.

    Structures Act s 41A
  6. Within a prescribed periodA development plan

    The new council must adopt an integrated development plan (IDP), or adopt its predecessor's, within a prescribed period after the start of its term. Until then, the previous council's plan stays in force.

    Systems Act s 25

How the votes work

  • Candidates are nominated on a form signed by two councillors, and the nominee must accept in writing. There is no debate.
  • If only one candidate is nominated, that person is declared elected.
  • If there is more than one, councillors present vote by secret ballot, one vote each. The winner needs a majority of the votes cast.
  • If nobody gets a majority, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and councillors vote again, until someone has a majority.
  • If the last two candidates tie, a further meeting must be held within seven days. If they tie again there, the winner is decided by lot.
  • More than half of all the council's councillors must be present for any vote to be taken.
Structures Act Schedule 3 · s 30(1)

Hung councils

When no party has more than half the seats

No party can elect a speaker or mayor on its own votes, so parties have to agree whom to back. Several things can then happen:

  • A majority coalition. Parties that together hold more than half the seats agree on a speaker and mayor, and vote them in.
  • A minority government. The winner needs a majority of the votes cast by the councillors present, not more than half of all seats. So a party or group short of a majority can still win the mayoral vote if its opponents split their votes or abstain.
  • A walkout. If so many councillors stay away that fewer than half of them are present, no vote can be taken and the meeting cannot elect anyone.
Structures Act s 30(1) · Schedule 3

Winning the mayoral vote is not the end of it. Passing the budget, setting rates and taxes, raising loans and passing by-laws all need the support of more than half of all councillors, not just of those voting. A minority government has to win those votes one by one.

Constitution s 160(2) and (3)(b) · Structures Act s 30

Deals can also unravel later. A council can remove its speaker, whip, mayor or executive mayor by a resolution of the council, and the law sets no limit on how often such motions can be brought.

Structures Act ss 40, 41E, 53, 58

Missed deadlines

What if there is no mayor after 14 days?

Nothing happens automatically. The Structures Act sets the deadlines, but it does not say what happens when a council misses them, and it does not regulate coalition agreements. The council can keep meeting until it elects its office-bearers.

In the meantime, the municipality's administration, headed by the municipal manager, keeps running. Decisions that need a mayor or the council stall.

Structures Act ss 29, 45, 55 · Systems Act s 55

If the stalemate drags on, the provincial government can step in. When a municipality cannot or does not fulfil an executive obligation, the province can issue a directive, take over that obligation itself, or, if exceptional circumstances warrant it, dissolve the council and appoint an administrator.

A dissolution has to be reported at once to the national minister for local government, the provincial legislature and the National Council of Provinces (NCOP). It takes effect 14 days after the NCOP receives the notice, unless the minister or the NCOP sets it aside before then.

Constitution s 139(1) and (3) · Structures Act s 34(4)

If a council cannot or does not approve a budget, the province must intervene, and that can include dissolving the council. The next budgets are due before the 2027/28 financial year starts on 1 July 2027.

Constitution s 139(4) · MFMA s 16

Dissolution

Dissolving a council

A council can dissolve itself only with a two-thirds vote at a meeting called for that purpose, and only once two years have passed since it was elected.

Structures Act s 34(1)-(2)

Otherwise, the province can dissolve a council only through the intervention route in section 139 of the Constitution, described above.

Structures Act s 34(4)

After a dissolution

If a council is dissolved, the MEC for local government must appoint one or more administrators to keep the municipality running until a new council is elected. The MEC must do the same if a council does not have enough members to form a quorum.

Structures Act s 35

A by-election for the whole council must then be held within 90 days of the dissolution, called by the MEC after consulting the IEC. The exception: no by-election is called if the next general municipal election is due within nine months, or if the MEC and the minister decide it should wait for that election.

Structures Act s 25(1)(c), (3) and (6)

Proposed law

The Coalitions Bill

The Municipal Structures Amendment Bill, often called the Coalitions Bill, was introduced in the National Assembly by the minister of cooperative governance on 18 August 2026. It would:

  • extend the deadlines for the first meeting and for electing a mayor or executive committee from 14 to 30 days;
  • require coalition agreements to be signed, submitted to the municipal manager and published in the Provincial Gazette; and
  • allow a motion to remove a speaker, whip, executive mayor or executive committee member only once every 12 months, unless there are grounds such as a breach of the Constitution, a criminal conviction or serious misconduct.

Like the current law, the bill does not say what happens if a council misses its deadlines.

It is not law. Parliament's cooperative governance committee was first briefed on it on 27 August and is taking public comment until 27 November 2026. It must then be passed by the National Assembly and the NCOP and signed by the President. So councils elected on 4 November must meet the current 14-day deadlines.

Municipal Structures Amendment Bill B23-2026 · Parliament and PMG, checked 9 November 2026
